stem: What is mass spectrometry? Write down its basic principle. Explain the construction and working of a mass spectrometer.
keyPoints: ["Mass spectrometry separates ions based on mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) to determine molecular mass","Molecules are ionized by high-energy electrons (70 eV) to form molecular ions (M⁺•) with m/z equal to relative molecular mass","Molecular ions are accelerated and separated in a magnetic field; lighter ions deflected more than heavier ions","Molecular ion peak appears at highest m/z value; fragmentation produces lower m/z peaks forming characteristic fingerprint pattern","Detector records ion abundance at each m/z value to produce mass spectrum for molecular identification"]
modelAnswer: Mass spectrometry is an analytical technique that separates ions based on their mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) to determine molecular mass and identify molecular structure. The basic principle involves ionizing chemical compounds to generate charged molecules or fragments, then separating these ions by their m/z values using electric and/or magnetic fields. A mass spectrometer consists of an ion source, accelerating region, mass analyzer, and detector. In operation, molecules are bombarded by high-energy electrons (70 eV) in the ion source, causing loss of an electron to form molecular ions (M⁺•). These ions are accelerated through an electric field, then separated in the mass analyzer based on their m/z ratios. Lighter ions are deflected more than heavier ions by the magnetic field. The detector records the abundance of ions at each m/z value, producing a mass spectrum. The molecular ion peak appears at the highest m/z value and indicates the relative molecular mass. Fragmentation of unstable molecular ions produces additional peaks at lower m/z values, creating a characteristic fragmentation pattern that serves as a fingerprint for molecular identification.
